text.p: High wages, excessive company taxes and a lumbering bureaucracy drove more foreign capital out of Germany in 1996 than in any other year since World War Two, an economic think-tank said on Tuesday.

Foreign companies withdrew a record net $3 billion in investment funds, making Germany the only developed country to record a net capital outflow, the Institute for the German Economy (IW) said in a report.
On a longer view, net direct foreign investment totalled $17.3 billion from 1991 to 1996, equal to just 0.6 percent of total investment in Germany.

"The catastrophic balance of foreign direct investment results from a fatal mix of high labour costs and business taxes, short working hours and over-regulation," IW economist Joerg Beyfuss said in the report.
The study by IW, which has close ties to big business, drew on recent findings by the Bundesbank.
The central bank said last week in its August report that, not only were foreign investors avoiding Germany, but domestic firms had also dramatically increased investment abroad since the 1980s.

The Bundesbank report said high business costs were just one of several reasons why net capital exports -- which ran at 0.5 to 0.75 percent of gross domestic product in the late 1980s and early 1990s -- had doubled in recent years.
It said rising investment by German firms abroad stemmed from the pressures of economic globalisation and efforts to produce goods nearer to the markets where they are sold.
But the central bank also cited information from companies which said high costs, heavy regulations and rigid labour markets were also deterrents to doing business in Germany.
"Further efforts in all these areas will be necessary to correct the false developments of the past and compete successfully against other developed industrialised countries," the Bundesbank wrote.

The IW said that, among mature economies, Germany outranked only Japan in terms of foreign investment as a share of total investment over the past five years. In Japan the figure was just 0.1 percent.
By contrast, foreign investment in European states like Belgium and Luxembourg made up 22.1 percent of the total, in Sweden 17 percent and in Britain 11.7 percent, the IW said, citing OECD data.
Foreign investment in Sweden as a share of the total rose by five times from 1991 to 1996, compared with the previous five years. In Germany it fell by 40 percent.
The IW said Sweden's success as a "magnet" for capital from abroad stemmed from welfare reforms, corporate tax cuts and a reduction of state interference.
"Meanwhile, economic policy in Germany is stuck in a dangerous blockade," the IW commented.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government has tried to battle record post-war unemployment, which it expects to average 4.3 million this year, with a combination of tax reforms, welfare changes and business deregulation.

But the government has backed off from ambitious plans to slash 30 billion marks ($16.4 billion) in income and corporate taxes after they were blocked by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) in parliament. It is now considering a more modest tax package.
Planned pensions reforms are unlikely to cut payroll costs by much and the loosening of restrictions on shop opening hours last year has failed to lift depressed retail sales.
"If the reform backlog is not cleared, we must fear that foreign capital will continue to make a detour around Germany," the IW said. ($ = 1.834 German Marks)
